recipe.history:
The chickpea — Cicer arietinum — is among the earliest cultivated legumes in human history, with archaeological evidence of its domestication dating to 7500 BCE in the southeastern Turkey region near the Karaçadağ Mountains, the same general area where wheat and lentils were first cultivated in the Neolithic agricultural revolution. From this origin, the chickpea spread eastward into the Indian subcontinent, where it became the foundation of dal and chana masala, and westward into the Middle East and Mediterranean, where it became the basis for hummus, falafel, and the beloved Spanish cocido. The Romans ate them enthusiastically — the name of the family Cicero derives from the Latin word for chickpea, cicer, which the historian Pliny attributed to a wart-like bump on the nose of one of the family's ancestors that resembled the legume. Chickpeas have nourished human civilization for nearly ten thousand years, and they have done so without asking for much in return: they fix nitrogen in the soil, grow in poor conditions, and provide complete protein when combined with grains.

Crispy roasted chickpeas — tossed in oil and spices and roasted at high heat until their skins split and their interiors turn dry and crunchy — arrived on American restaurant menus in the early 2010s as a bar snack and salad topping, riding the wave of Mediterranean-inspired cuisine that was making harissa and labneh and za'atar familiar to American diners. Their application as a burger topping followed quickly: chefs discovered that a handful of crispy chickpeas on a beef patty provided the same crunch as fried shallots or panko breadcrumbs while adding a nutty, slightly earthy flavor that complemented beef in a way that was distinctly different from anything in the traditional burger topping repertoire. Paired with a tahini sauce — sesame paste thinned with lemon and garlic — the chickpeas create a Middle Eastern-inflected burger that honors the legume's cultural origins while fitting naturally into the format of an American sandwich.

I roast chickpeas at least twice a month now, which is more than I had expected when I first tried them. I started because a recipe instructed me to use them as a salad topping, and I ended up eating the entire baking sheet standing at the kitchen counter, one small crispy chickpea at a time, before the salad was assembled. There is something compulsive about them: the snap, the nuttiness, the way the spice coating intensifies in the oven into something more complex than the sum of its parts. I started adding them to things that had no precedent for chickpeas — grain bowls, soups, flatbreads — and then eventually to a burger, where the combination with the beef was so immediately satisfying that I felt I had discovered something rather than invented it. That feeling — the feeling that a combination was always there and you simply had not found it yet — is one of the best feelings cooking offers.

Medium rare is the only rational temperature for this burger, and the logic is structural as much as culinary. Crispy roasted chickpeas will absorb moisture if given the chance — a wet surface, a steamy environment, and they lose their crunch within minutes. A medium rare patty at 130–135°F (54–57°C) is warm but not steaming: it does not produce the kind of sustained moisture release that a well-done patty does when its squeezed-out juices pool in the base of the bun. Medium rare means the patty retains its juices internally, so the chickpeas stay crispy on top, the tahini sauce stays creamy in the middle, and the whole burger maintains its textural integrity from first bite to last. This is not a small thing. Crunch is a fundamental pleasure, and it deserves to be protected.
ingredients: 3 large eggs (2 for dough, 1 for egg wash)
2 cans (800g total drained weight) chickpeas, drained and rinsed
0.5 small red onion, very thinly sliced
900g freshly ground beef (80% chuck, 20% brisket blend)
instructions: 1. Roast the crispy chickpeas (can be done up to a day ahead): Preheat oven to 220°C (425°F). Drain and rinse chickpeas thoroughly, then spread on a clean kitchen towel and pat very dry — this is critical for crispiness. Remove any loose skins. Transfer to a baking sheet, drizzle with olive oil, and toss to coat. Roast for 20 minutes, shaking the pan halfway through. Remove from the oven, toss with cumin, smoked paprika, coriander, garlic powder, cayenne, salt, and pepper, then return to the oven for 10–15 more minutes until deeply golden, split, and audibly crunchy. Cool on the pan — they will continue to crisp as they cool. Store uncovered at room temperature until needed.

2. Make the tahini sauce: Combine tahini, lemon juice, grated garlic, ground cumin, and kosher salt in a bowl and whisk. The mixture will initially seize and become thick. Add cold water one tablespoon at a time, whisking after each addition, until the sauce reaches a smooth, creamy, pourable consistency — similar to thick cream. Taste and adjust lemon, salt, and garlic. Refrigerate until needed but bring to room temperature before serving.
3. Make the harissa yogurt: Stir together Greek yogurt, harissa paste, and lemon juice until evenly combined. Season with salt. Refrigerate until needed.

4. Make the brioche buns: Combine bread flour, instant yeast, salt, and sugar in a stand mixer with a dough hook. Add 2 eggs and warm milk, mix on low for 2 minutes, then knead on medium for 5 minutes. Add softened butter one tablespoon at a time, fully incorporating each addition. Knead on medium-high for 8 minutes until smooth and elastic.

5. Place dough in a lightly oiled bowl, cover, and let rise 1 hour until doubled. Divide into 6 portions of about 100g, shape into tight balls, place on parchment-lined baking sheets, and proof covered for 45 minutes.
6. Preheat oven to 190°C (375°F). Brush buns with egg wash (remaining egg plus 1 tablespoon water) and sprinkle with sesame seeds. Bake for 16–18 minutes until deep golden. Cool on a wire rack.
7. If using halloumi: slice into 6 pieces about 8mm thick. Heat a dry non-stick skillet over high heat and cook halloumi slices for 2 minutes per side until deeply golden. Set aside.

8. Make the herb salad: Just before assembly, combine parsley, mint, cilantro, and sliced red onion in a bowl. Whisk olive oil and lemon juice together, season with salt and pepper, and dress the herbs lightly.

9. Form the beef patties: Combine ground beef, ground cumin, salt, and cracked pepper. Mix gently just to distribute. Divide into 6 portions of 150g. Handle minimally. Form into 10cm-wide, 2cm-thick patties with a thumb indent in the center.

10. Heat a cast-iron skillet over high heat until smoking. Cook patties dry and undisturbed for 3 minutes. Flip once. If using halloumi, place a slice on each patty. Cook for 2–2.5 more minutes. Confirm the center reads 130–135°F (54–57°C) for medium rare. Rest on a wire rack for 3 minutes.
11. Slice brioche buns and toast cut-side down in a buttered skillet over medium heat for 60–90 seconds.

12. Assemble each burger: Spread harissa yogurt on the bottom bun and tahini sauce on the top bun. Place cucumber slices and tomato slices on the bottom bun. Set the rested patty (with halloumi if using) on top. Drizzle a spoonful of extra tahini sauce directly over the patty. Top with a generous handful of crispy spiced chickpeas. Crown with the herb salad. Dust with a pinch of sumac and flaky sea salt. Cap with the top bun and serve immediately while the chickpeas are still crisp.
